title: The soul as a bride
hook: many hymns speak as a bride longing for her Husband Lord, a picture of the soul's love

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, the ease that comes when the grip lets go. Your line was ease. Did one ordinary thing go slowly and easily? Today, the Granth's warmest picture of the soul. Day two hundred forty-four.

Here's something that surprises people the first time they hear it. The ten Gurus were all men. And yet, again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, they sing in a woman's voice. A young bride, waiting at the window. Getting ready, wondering if her beloved will come. Asking her friends how they won his love. Guru Nanak does it. Guru Arjan does it. Kabir does it too. Why would the Gurus choose that voice, of all voices, to speak about God? Today's word opens it: suhagan.
screen: `THE GURUS WERE MEN.` → `THEY SING AS A BRIDE.` → `WHY THAT VOICE?`

segments.voice: Suhagan means the happily married bride, the one united with her husband. Its opposite in the hymns is duhagan, the bride left alone, forgotten. In this picture, God is the Husband, the Beloved, and every soul is the bride, whether the person singing is a man or a woman. It's not a statement about men and women. It's a picture of love. Think about what a bride in the old Punjab knew. She couldn't earn her husband's love by arguing or bargaining. She could get ready, keep faith, and wait. So the hymns ask: how does a bride become suhagan? Not through jewelry, not through fancy clothes, they say, but through humility, sweet speech, and love. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns, the bride asks the happy wives what they did, and the answer is, roughly, give up your pride, and let him have his way. That's hukam, the order, turned into romance. The picture reaches its height at a Sikh wedding. The Laavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung while the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib. They're a wedding song, and they're also about the soul's marriage to God, stage by stage. So every Sikh wedding is two weddings at once. And there's something tender in it for anyone. It says the deepest thing between a person and God isn't fear or duty. It's longing, and belonging.
screen: `SUHAGAN — THE UNITED BRIDE.` · `EVERY SOUL IS THE BRIDE.` · `NOT JEWELS — HUMILITY AND LOVE.` · `THE LAAVAN: TWO WEDDINGS AT ONCE.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS A BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen, or the notes on your phone. Write one line of longing. It can be for God, if that's your language, or for peace, for someone you miss, for the person you hope to become. Just one honest line, in your own words: I wish, I miss, I'm waiting for. Read it once, quietly. Then set it down and sit with the feeling it leaves, without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
Suhagan. The bride united with her beloved. In the Granth, a picture of the soul, any soul, joined with God through love and humility.
Your line: the soul is a bride. Today, keep the line of longing you wrote somewhere you'll see it again tonight. Day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: At a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the four verses of the Laavan by Guru Ram Das are read and sung as the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib, and they're understood as describing both the marriage and the soul's union with God.

fork.reveal: the answer is humility and surrender to his will, hukam told as a love story.

original.note: Gurmukhi: suhagan, the happily married bride; from suhag, the good fortune of a married woman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bride is just a wedding picture.
what it means: in the Granth, every soul is a bride, and union with God comes through love and humility, not ornaments or argument.
what a scholar hears: suhagan and duhagan, from suhag, marital good fortune; a devotional convention shared with Sufi and bhakti poetry, where the male poet takes the woman's voice.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 773–774 (Suhi Mahala 4, the Laavan)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1107–1110 (Tukhari Mahala 1, Barah Maha: the bride through the twelve months)
Guru Granth Sahib, Tilang Mahala 1 (the bride asks the happy wives; around Ang 722)

notes: The hymn where the bride asks the happy wives how they won the Husband (jaae puchhahu sohaaganee) is attributed to Guru Nanak in Tilang, around Ang 722; confirm the Ang and the paraphrase ('give up your pride, let him have his way').
Laavan cited as Suhi Mahala 4, Ang 773–774; confirm.
The note that the bridal voice is a convention shared with Sufi and bhakti poetry is stated as a scholarly observation, without ranking; confirm wording.
Suhagan etymology from suhag (marital good fortune) is standard; confirm spelling ਸੁਹਾਗਣਿ as used in Gurbani.
